 STAR1 - 3D version without design
 STAR2 - 2D version with design

 Effects of 3rd order theory are available for truss and cable elements.
 The static system must be described by the user in terms of discrete elements, and the corre- sponding database must be defined by the generation program.
 Available elements are:
 • Beam element with straight axis and step-by-step constant arbitrary cross section. Analysis by 2nd order theory with consideration of the shear deformation. Consideration of non- linear material behaviour through iteration.
 • Spring element such as support spring or node-coupling spring; non-linear effects include slip, failure, yielding and friction.
 • Truss element with prestress
 • Cable element with prestress (only tensile force is possible)
 • Distributed support element for elastic support of beams
 • Couplings for special effects like eccentric beam links, rigid links between nodes etc.
 Disk or plate elements as well as solid elements, which can be defined by the generation program, can not be processed by STAR2. The foundation definitions for pile elements are not available in STAR2 either.
 Concentrated forces or moments may act on the nodes, while support translations or rotations can be defined at any support. The beam elements can be loaded with point loads at any po- sition in the form of eccentrically acting forces, moments, jumps in displacement or rotation, as well as with linearly varying loads in the form of forces, moments, strains, curvatures or temper- ature strains. Unintentional eccentricities of linear, quadratic or cubic variation can be defined for the analysis with 2nd order theory. In addition, creep deformations or unintentional eccen- tricities can be generated from already analysed load cases. Prestress can be considered by specifying an MV0 or NV0 distribution.
 The analysis of frames by 2nd order theory with consideration of material behaviour is a de- manding engineering task. The user of STAR2 should therefore accumulate experience from simple examples, before attempting to take on more complicated structures. A check of the results by off-hand engineering calculations is indispensable.

The static problem is solved by the deformation method. In any iterative technique, non-linear properties must be decomposed into several individual linear steps by an iterative method. A closed form solution can be computed by 2nd order theory for such a linear step, if the stiffness and the axial force are assumed constant.

The program uses exclusively right-handed coordinate systems in accordance to DIN 1080 for the description of force-, moment-, displacement- or rotation-vectors. The three-dimensional global system of coordinates serves in defining the nodal coordinates and displacements or rotations.
 Each beam gets a local coordinate system, which is defined by the generation program. Beam deformations and internal forces and moments are output in this coordinate system. When confusion is possible, the local xyz-system is also designated by S12.

The separate analysis in the primary and secondary direction is correct only when the axes y and z are the principal axes of the cross section. If this condition is not satisfied, the deforma- tions are not computed correctly in case of statically determinate structures, whereas in case of statically indeterminate structures the internal forces and moments are wrong too. STAR2 transforms all the loads and the internal forces of three- dimensional structures into the direc- tions of the principal axes. Variable rotation along the length of a beam can not be considered however. This transformation can be suppressed in special cases. The principal axes are
 always taken into consideration correctly during design, when biaxial bending is active.

The image is a labeled schematic illustrating three force–displacement (P–V) behaviors for springs, presented side-by-side as parts of “Figure 2.2: Force-displacement diagrams of springs.” Across the top of each sub-figure, the vertical axis is labeled **P** (force) with an upward arrow indicating positive force direction. Along the horizontal axis, the variable is labeled **V** (displacement) with an arrow pointing to the right indicating positive displacement.

**Left sub-figure (GAP behavior):**  
This panel shows a force diagram with a **dead zone or gap**. A horizontal reference line is drawn across the mid-height, and two vertical markers indicate **“GAP”** on both sides (left and lower-left). The force remains essentially zero (or does not activate) until displacement reaches the gap limit. After this threshold, the force increases in a **linear sloped line** starting from the gap boundary, indicating an initially inactive spring region followed by linear stiffness activation.

**Middle sub-figure (Failure/YIELD reference with nonlinear activation):**  
The center panel shows a **stiffer linear segment** that transitions to a **different response**. There is a sloped line rising from the origin/reference toward a marked point where the slope changes. Near the transition point there is an annotation-like symbol (appearing as a crack-like or label mark) adjacent to the sloped line. A vertical line labeled **“FAIL”** (with text partially stylized) indicates a failure threshold. After that point, the diagram changes to a horizontal/plateau-like segment, suggesting that once the failure condition is reached, the spring loses its load-carrying capability (force drops to a reduced or zero level). An additional small vertical reference line appears near the right side, implying a continuation or second threshold condition.

**Right sub-figure (YIELD behavior):**  
The right panel shows the continuation of a nonlinear material/spring response involving **yield**. A vertical annotation on the left side of the panel reads **“+ YIELD”** (with a plus sign visible), and a corresponding horizontal segment suggests yielding occurs at a certain force level. The diagram includes a sloped line that rises, then transitions into a **reduced-slope or plateau region** consistent with yield: force can increase further but with a different stiffness than in the initial elastic range. A plus sign and the word “YIELD” are clearly shown near the upper part of the panel.

Overall, the schematic visually summarizes common nonlinear spring effects referenced in the accompanying context—particularly **prestress-related activation thresholds (GAP)**, and non-linear limits such as **failure** and **yield**. The figure emphasizes piecewise-linear behavior: initial inactive or elastic response, then changes at defined threshold conditions labeled by **GAP**, **FAIL**, and **+YIELD**.

The image is a two-panel schematic (left and right) illustrating iteration methods labeled **a** and **b** for determining the force–displacement response of a spring element during **non-linear analysis**. It includes axes and piecewise linear/constructed lines to show how the “secant stiffness” is obtained from iterative computations.

### Left panel (method a)
- The horizontal axis is labeled **V** (displacement), and the vertical axis is labeled **P** (force).
- Two straight black lines originate from the origin: one is a steeper line (associated with an initial/stiffer tangent behavior) and another is a less steep line (associated with a reduced stiffness after accounting for nonlinearity).
- There are additional thin/offset markings indicating an intermediate displacement level (a vertical dashed line rises from the displacement value on the V-axis to a point on a line).
- A **circle/marker** labeled **E** (shown near the upper region) sits on one of the rising lines, suggesting an “effective” stiffness point used for the iteration.
- The diagram shows a local secant relationship between the origin and the computed intersection point: the resulting line segment has slope corresponding to the stiffness computed for that iteration.
- Small text/labels near the sloped lines include **E₀** and **Eₛ**, implying an “initial” stiffness (E₀) and a “secant” or “secant stiffness” (Eₛ).

### Right panel (method b)
- The axes are the same: **P** vertical, **V** horizontal.
- This panel shows the inverse control scenario compared to method a.
- The construction is shifted so that a **horizontal reference line** at a prescribed force level intersects the sloped response lines.
- A **vertical dashed line** then projects from the intersection down to the V-axis, indicating that displacement is determined based on the prescribed force.
- Two lines again represent different stiffness states, with a reduced or altered slope due to nonlinearity.
- Labels **E₀** and **Eₛ** again appear near the stiffness-related lines, and a marker near the intersection indicates the point used to compute the secant stiffness.

### Overall meaning
The figure caption reads: **“Figure 2.3: iteration methods a / b”**. The left panel visualizes **strain control (a):** for a prescribed displacement, the corresponding force is determined by iteration (secant stiffness obtained from computed force–displacement). The right panel visualizes **stress control (b):** for a prescribed force, the corresponding displacement is determined by iteration. In both cases, the effective stiffness used by the solver is the slope derived from the constructed secant relationship between origin and the converged/iteration intersection point.

Spring elements model structural parts by a simplified force- displacement relationship. This is usually expressed by means of a spring constant in the form of a linear equation:
 P = c ·
 (2.18)
 The spring is defined by its direction ( DX, DY, DZ ) and the spring constants. The direction can be determined as the difference of two nodes (N2 - NA), or it can be specified explicitly. Support springs must be provided with a direction (see generation program). The element implemented herein allows for the following non-linear effects:
 - Prestress (linear effect)
 - Failure
 - Yield
 - Friction with cohesion
 - Slip
 Geometrically non-linear effects are not possible for springs.
 A prestress shifts the corresponding effects and it always generates a loading upon the struc- ture. A prestressed spring is relaxed in the absence of external loading or compulsion. The non-linear effects apply to rotational springs as well as lateral springs too. Friction can be defined by a lateral spring. The force components normal to the spring’s direction of action are equal to the product of the displacement components in the lateral direction by the lateral spring constants. This force is at most equal to the product of the force in the normal direction by the friction coefficient plus the cohesion. If the normally oriented spring is eliminated, the lateral spring is automatically eliminated too.
 All spring non-linearities are activated only during a non-linear analysis. To this end, a value for the number of iterations must be specified by the analysis methods in CTRL.
 Upon such request (see input record CTRL) either the force corresponding to a prescribed displacement value will be determined within an iteration (strain control a) or the displacement for a prescribed force (stress control b). A secant stiffness results from the values computed in this way. Method a should be used by structures, which soften as they are loaded, whereas
 method b should be used for stiffening structural members.
 The user must take care so that the system does not become unstable in any step of the iteration through failure of springs or cables. This can happen, for instance,if one defines additional springs with small stiffness, resulting to a small remaining stiffness after the main spring’s failure. This stiffness should not be less than the stiffness of the main spring divided by 10000.

Trusses can be analysed by 2nd or 3rd order theory. 2nd order theory is considered as de- scribed in /9/; nodal deformations are additionally taken into account in the construction of the element matrices by 3rd order theory.

Cable elements are handled similarly to trusses. Cables can not sustain any compressive forces. 2nd and 3rd order theories are applicable as for trusses. A correct computation is generally possible through several iterations only.
 In order to analyse a cable structure, which is usually stable only under loading, by 1st order theory too, it is assumed that the elements are subjected to a small prestress.

A global stiffness matrix is obtained by adding all the individual element stiffnesses; after in- corporating the geometric boundary conditions, the displacements and thus the internal forces get computed. If non-linear springs or a redistribution of the axial force are present, the input of a number of iterations within the defined limits will force the whole process to be repeated by updating the secant stiffnesses until a solution is obtained.

The number of load cases is limited to 999.
 The number of nodes, beams, sections or loads is only limited by the amount of the available disk space. 5 digits are usually reserved for the output of their numbers, thus values above
 99999 should not be used.
 STAR2 works with double precision. Despite that the following points should be considered:
 1. The stiffness EI/l3 of neighbouring beam elements may not differ by a factor larger
 than 10-5.
 2. Beam theory is valid only for structural members, the length of which is at least twice their height. The length of each individual element should not be smaller than the height of the cross section used.
 3. Artificially rigid elements can and must be defined as couplings.
 If these criteria are not met, reaction forces will arise on free nodes.
 STAR2 sets a constant stiffness for each segment. The buckling length coefficient β after Pe- tersen /6/ p.489 reaches a maximum of 1.22 for a conical beam under its own weight compared to 1.12 for a prismatic beam (8% error). If the dimensions are changed by just 10% (I-Value by 27.1%), β reaches 1.14, corresponding to an error of about 2%.

Initial deformations (unintentional eccentricities) are deviations of the actual beam axis from the ideal beam axis. These are independent of self-arising deformations. They have no effect on an analysis by 1st order theory.
 The following variations are possible:
 Linear inclination (e.g. DIN 1045 Sec. 15.8.2)
 Input in the form of a point load at the column head.
 Arbitrary step-by-step linear variation.
 Input in the form of distributed load.
 Arbitrary shape related to the buckling mode (e.g. DIN 1045 17.4). Defined either by several positions along the column, connected by a cubic spline, or by the bending line from an already analysed load case.

DIN 1045 requires an estimation of the effects of creep and shrinkage according to Section 17.4, when the slenderness of the compressed member is greater than 70 for immovable or 45 for movable structures and at the same time the eccentricity e/d is smaller than 2.
 Creep deformations are computed for the permanent loads acting in the service state as well as for any prescribed permanent beam deflections and eccentricities including the unintentional ones.
 An approximate method using an increased unintentional eccentricity is described in note 220 of DAfSt.
 STAR2, however, can perform a more accurate check. A load case is built for this purpose from the loads that cause creep. The resulting deformations, multiplied by a creep factor, can be
 used either as initial deformations or as curvature loads during a subsequent run. The same method allows the consideration of construction phases.

A fixed prestress can be specified in the generation program for springs and trusses. This acts by every load case and generates corresponding stresses. A prestress for each individual load case can be defined in STAR2 as well.
 A statically determinate component of the prestress (NV0,MV0) for each load case can be defined separately for bending beams. Then, depending on the number of parameters, any variation of these values from constant to cubic can be assumed along the beam axis. The effect of prestress is twofold. On one hand, the internal forces and moments are modified by the corresponding prestress values, and on the other hand, deformations result from prestress, which in turn lead to compulsory forces in cases of statically indeterminate structures.
 Prestress is considered differently for cables and for beam elements. A cable or a truss can be only prestressed through the external system. Therefore, the prestress is then analysed like a temperature stressing caused by a strain imposed on the element. Forces are generated within the elements of an undeformed structure, whereas in deformed structures the prestress deteriorates due to self-arising deformations. If one wants to receive a defined prestress, one must employ therefore an element with very small strain stiffness.
 For beams, by contrast, prestress is defined as an independent state of stress (prestressed concrete). Since the prestress is imposed on the element itself, the resulting forces on freely deformable beams are the input internal forces themselves. If the deformation is hindered, compulsory forces arise. In the limiting case, e.g. if a beam is prevented from deforming in the longitudinal direction, the resulting axial force is null, because the forces imposed by the prestressing steel are resisted by the support instead of the beam.

The shear deformation can be also taken into account by the beam elements. The program AQUA defines the standard shear areas for some cross sections. The internal force variation in statically indeterminate structures may differ from the one obtained by pure bending theory, if shear deformation is taken into consideration.

Since the design or stiffness computation by AQB must be activated for an iteration with non- linear material behaviour after any static analysis, the most important records of AQB are also available in STAR2. These are:
 CTRL - General parameter
 REIN
 - Special parameter for DESI and NSTR
 DESI - Reinforcement computation
 NSTR
 - Strain state
 The complete theory for these records can be found in the AQB manual. Only the descriptions of the input records are given in this manual.
 If not all of the beams are to be dimensioned in the same way, this can be avoided by an external iteration via the record processor PS.

The input is made in the CADINP language (see general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUC- TURAL Installation and Basics’). Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

### Table purpose and scope
This table lists **record definitions and their allowable “items”** for the SOFiSTiK input block that includes **CTRL**-controlled analysis/design/stiffness computation. It focuses on how different records (e.g., `ECHO`, `CTRL`, `GRP`, `INFL`, `LC`, `LCC`, `LV`, `*REIN`, `*DESI`, `*NSTR`) accept named parameters. Conceptually, these records appear within the **standard input structure** described in the surrounding context: the program processes input in **blocks terminated by `ENDE`**, stops when an **empty block** is found, and distinguishes **load generation vs analysis vs restart** runs through presence/absence of records like `CTRL` and loads.

### Structural logic implied by the table
Each row corresponds to a **record keyword**. Under each record, the table enumerates **item keywords** that can be supplied as part of that record. The presence of an asterisk (e.g., `*REIN`, `*DESI`, `*NSTR`) indicates a set of records that are specifically tied to **design/strain computation** and the **AQB** subsystem (as referenced in the context). The record grouping also signals that some entries are primarily **analysis control**, while others are **design-related parameters**.

### Record-by-record description
- **`ECHO`**
  - Items: `OPT`, `VAL`, `SELE`
  - Purpose: likely controls echo/output selection related to options and values (used to control reporting verbosity or targeted result display).

- **`CTRL`** (central analysis method control)
  - Items: `OPT`, `VAL`
  - It is followed by a second header line showing additional configuration entries relevant to control and stiffness computation (as referenced in the context).
  - The context explains that `CTRL` defines parameters such as:
    - references to primary load cases for **second-order stiffness computation** (`PLC`/`PLF` logic),
    - options like `LIT CABL` / `CABL` (tension-only cables), `TRUS` (allow compression in cables),
    - `DRUC` (deactivation of second-order effects for certain tensile beam conditions),
    - `GDIV` (group divisor),
    - treatment for **nonlinear stiffness selection** for beam elements.
  - Therefore, this row indicates `CTRL` is not a mere input flag; it is a **method switchboard** driving nonlinear/second-order analysis behavior.

- **`GRP`**

The input table defines parameters for a load-case record (LC-related), including how elements are grouped, how stiffness and cross-section properties are interpreted, and how additional modifiers (presprestress, shear centre, dead weight, construction stage) affect the analysis. The table is organized as rows of “Item” (parameter name) with a textual “Description”, “Unit”, and “Default” value.

Key field **NO** represents the “Group number” identifier used to address which element group the record applies to. Its unit is not given (shown as “–”) and no explicit default is listed (“–”).

A second parameter **VAL** controls whether and how group selection is used. It accepts literals:
- **OFF**: do not use
- **YES**: use
- **FULL**: use and print results  
The default for VAL is **FULL**, meaning group selection is active and results are printed. The default unit column lists **LIT** (literal/enum), indicating a categorical choice rather than a numeric quantity.

The field **STIF** (“Stiffness parameters”) configures stiffness-related modeling options:
- **1**: consider rotation of principal axes
- **0**: do not consider rotation  
Additionally it provides special modes for designed vs. non-designed groups:
- **LIN1**: “1 + not designed group”
- **LIN0**: “0 + not designed group”  
Default is **1**. This parameter thus determines whether principal-axis rotation is incorporated in the stiffness formulation and can control treatment of groups that are not designed.

The field **SECT** selects which cross-section quantity is used:
- **BRUT**: effective gross cross section (default selection symbolized by LIT)
- **TOTA**: total cross section
- **DESI**: design cross section based on a factor of \(1/\gamma_m\) (material safety factor application)
The table marks the default as **LIT** (with an asterisk indicating a non-numeric default selection policy). Context text further clarifies that the governing program typically defaults to “cooperating cross section” for cross-section values, and that “area” is substituted by total cross section.

**SC** (“Shear centre”) controls shear-centre consideration:
- **NONE**: do not consider
- **YES**: consider by loads only
- **FULL**: consider fully  
Default is **FULL**.

**PRES** (“Prestress loading”) selects the components of prestress effects to include:
- **FULL**: consider all effects (default)
- **NOTO**: exclude torsional components
- **REST**: include only statically indeterminate components
- **UNRE**: include only statically determinate components
- **URNT**: combination of UNRE + NOTO (as stated)  
Default is **FULL**.

Modifier factors include:
- **FACS**: “Factor of linear stiffnesses”, default **1.0**
- **FACG**: “Dead weight factor”, default **1.0**  
These factors scale stiffness and dead weight contributions for the affected element group (per the provided context: FACG acts as an additional multiplier to element dead-weight loads DLX–DLZ in the LC record).

Finally, **CS** (“Construction stage number”) has default “–” (no numeric default specified). **FACP** (“Factor of prestress”) is shown with default **1.0**, scaling prestress effects.

The table defines a minimal set of inputs for the program record **LC – Definition of a Load Case**, i.e., parameters used to create/identify a load case for structural analysis and for later superposition or postprocessing.

### Columns
- **Item**: Row identifier for each input field.
- **Description**: Meaning of the field and what it controls in the LC record.
- **Unit**: Engineering unit (here mostly “-”, indicating no physical unit).
- **Default**: Default value applied when the field is omitted.

### Fields (rows)

1. **NO — Load case number (1–999)**
   - **Purpose**: Assigns the numeric identifier of the load case that is created or updated by the LC input.
   - **Valid range**: 1 to 999.
   - **Unit**: none (dimensionless identifier).
   - **Default**: **1**.
   - **Context/behavior**: This load case number is also used to link related commands (e.g., when defining influence lines via **INFL**, the INFL record references a load copy that is based on earlier **SOFILOAD** definitions). In workflows, specifying **LC** establishes which loading data apply to that case number and how updates/deletions of previously stored loads behave.

2. **TITL — Title of influence line load case**
   - **Purpose**: Provides a human-readable title/label for an **influence line** load case, improving database readability and interpretation in output/postprocessing.
   - **Unit**: none.
   - **Default**: **LIT24** (a placeholder/system default title).
   - **Context/behavior**: Although the record is described for influence line load cases, it functions as metadata for the LC entry and is useful when multiple INFL computations are generated (typically one per point of interest).

### Overall interpretation for RAG use
This table is best viewed as the **header/metadata mapping** for the LC record, where **NO** is the key that uniquely identifies the load case to the analysis engine, and **TITL** optionally tags influence line cases for clarity. The broader LC behavior (importing old loads with a factor, deleting previously stored loads when new loads are provided, and orchestrating analysis via subsequent commands like STAR2) is implied by the surrounding documentation, but the table itself only specifies the two fields and their defaults.

The input table summarizes how **influence lines** are obtained and what kind of **required “loading” or displacement/rotation setting** corresponds to each structural response quantity. It has three columns: **Influence line** (response type), **Required loading** (the specific unit action that must be applied to compute that influence line), and **e.g.** (examples of how the corresponding unit action is specified in SOFiLOAD/SOFILOAD-like commands).

1) **Moment My → Required loading: Unit rotation**  
   To compute an influence line for the bending moment **My**, the model activates a **unit rotation** as the driving quantity. In the “e.g.” column, the table indicates this can be done using a beam end/element load pattern such as **BEPL DY** with the appropriate scaling/unit interpretation (the surrounding context text shows that BEPL with TYPE DY is used for unit rotation setups).

2) **Axial force Nx → Required loading: Unit displacement**  
   For the influence line of the axial force **Nx**, the required driving quantity is a **unit displacement**. The example lists **BEPL WX**, implying a beam element point load definition tied to an axial-related deformation mode (WX type in the context typically corresponds to a displacement/rotation mapping used to derive axial effects).

3) **Shear force Vz → Required loading: Unit displacement**  
   The influence line for the shear force **Vz** also requires a **unit displacement** driving action. The example shows **BEPL WZ**, analogous to the Nx case but mapped to shear/deformation component WZ. Both Nx and Vz therefore use unit displacements, but with different deformation component identifiers.

4) **Support reaction → Required loading: Nodal displacement**  
   Influence lines for **support reactions** are computed using **nodal displacement** as the unit driving quantity. The example indicates the command structure **NODE WXX, WY Y, WZZ** (as written in the table) to select the proper nodal displacement component(s) corresponding to the reaction direction. This aligns with influence-line concepts where reactions depend on node kinematics.

5) **Displacement → Required loading: Unit load**  
   For the influence line of a **displacement** response itself, the table states the required loading is a **unit load**. The examples show **STEL PX, PY, PZ**, meaning unit point (or element) loads applied in local directions. This makes sense because a displacement influence line is the structural response caused by a unit external force.

Overall, the table provides a mapping between **what response you want in the influence line** and **what unit excitation you must define** when creating an **INFL load case** (as described in the context text: “INFL is computed based on corresponding loading patterns” and “for each point of interest, a separate load case INFL must be defined”).

The table defines the input record **LC – “Definition of a Load Case”**. It specifies how a load case number is created/managed in the structural analysis program, including global scaling, dead-load multipliers, naming, action/type classification, safety/combinations, and three generic criteria parameters used later for postprocessing.

### Key fields
- **NO (Load case number, 1–9999)**: Identifies the load case. **Default = 1**. Special value **LC ALL** means: compute all linear and nonlinear load cases stored in the database.
- **FACT (Factor for all loads of type P and M)**: Applies as a *global temporary scaling* to forces (**P**) and moments (**M**) within this load case. **Default = 1**. If FACT is used, it effectively creates/copies loads into a new load case context; it does **not** additionally modify DLX/DLY/DLZ unless those are explicitly controlled as well.
- **DLX, DLY, DLZ (dead load factors)**: Scalar multipliers for dead loads in the **x**, **y**, and **z** directions, respectively. Each has **Default = 0**. These interact with the record **GRP** via additional stiffness/weight factors (see context text): the factors for dead load are taken over only if corresponding dead-load factors are defined (otherwise dead loads may come from earlier inputs or from SOFiLOAD depending on how LC is used).
- **TITL (Title of load case)**: Descriptive label. **Default = LIT24**.
- **TYPE (Type/Action of load case)**: Categorical/action definition. The actual meaning is later detailed in the separate **ACT** record of program **SOFiLOAD** (context text). **Default is not stated** in the table (shown as “–”). Additional safety/combination coefficients can be overridden here depending on needs.
- **GAMU, GAMF, PSI0, PS11, PS12, PS1S, GAMAA**: Safety factors and combination coefficients:
  - **GAMU (Unfavourable safety factor)**  
  - **GAMF (Favourable safety factor)**
  - **PSI0** rare combination value  
  - **PS11** frequent combination value frequent  
  - **PS12** quasi-permanent combination value  
  - **PS1S** non-frequent combination value  
  - **GAMA** accidental safety factor  
  For these entries, the table marks defaults as “*” (i.e., the program default depends on system configuration or associated SOFiLOAD/MAXIMA logic rather than a fixed numeric value).
- **CRI1, CRI2, CRI3 (Criteria I–III)**: Three generic parameters (all unitless “–”). **Default = 0** for each. The context specifies they are used freely for postprocessing via DBVIEW; one explicit usage is that **TALPA uses CRI1** as a safety factor criterion for Fellenius-based analysis.

### Behavioral notes captured by the context
- Entering **LC** initiates the analysis or defines the load case.
- If **LC** contains only global scaling (e.g., FACT) and is not followed by explicit loads, previously stored loads for the same load case can be imported and scaled.
- If **some loads follow LC** (or if dead weight is redefined), the program first **deletes other loads stored under the same load case number**, then stores the new set.
- For restarts of nonlinear calculations with **NSTR**, the context indicates **LC must not be indicated**, otherwise nonlinear strains would be extinguished.

The input table defines parameter fields for **LV – “Generating Loads from Results of a Load Case”**. LV creates loading for a new analysis step by importing previously stored results (from an earlier STAR2 analysis) as *equivalent loads*, enabling investigations such as creep effects, support changes across construction phases, and initial deformations (e.g., system imperfections). Only **beam, truss, and cable element results** within specified selection ranges are imported.

### Field-by-field meaning
- **NO** *(Number of a loadcase; unit: “–”, default: “–”)*  
  Specifies the **source load case number** whose stored results are used. It can be up to **999**. LV uses this load case to retrieve beam/truss/cable results that will be transformed into loads.

- **FACT** *(Factor for load values; default: 1)*  
  A **multiplier applied to the imported load values** originating from the selected load case. If FACT is not changed, the imported effects are used with a factor of **1**. This allows different creep factors or scaling for different LV entries.

- **FROM / TO** *(Range data for beam numbers; default: FROM = “–”, TO = “FROM”)*  
  These define the **selection interval of beam element identifiers** whose results are imported.  
  - **FROM**: first beam number in the range  
  - **TO**: last beam number in the range  
  The default behavior sets **TO = FROM**, implying a single beam if only FROM is provided.

- **INC** *(Increment for beam numbers; default: 1)*  
  Step size within the beam number range. For example, INC = 2 would import every second beam number in the FROM–TO interval.

- **NFR0 / NTO / NINC** *(Range data for node numbers; defaults: NTO = NFR0, NINC = 1)*  
  The table provides analogous range-selection for **nodes** involved in importing or filtering node-related data for LV.  
  - **NFR0**: first node number  
  - **NTO**: last node number (default equals NFR0)  
  - **NINC**: node number increment (default 1)

- **TFRO / TTO / TINC** *(Range data for truss-bar numbers; defaults: TTO = TFRO, TINC = 1)*

The table defines input parameters for **LV – “Generating Loads from Results of a Load Case”** in STAR2. LV allows stored **beam results from earlier STAR2 analyses** to be **processed as loads** in a new analysis step. This is used for investigations such as **creep effects**, **support changes due to construction phases**, and **generation of initial deformations** (e.g., system imperfections). Only **beam, truss, and cable elements** within a specified range can be imported. The table specifies how to select which earlier load case to read, which elements it applies to, and how to transform the stored elastic line into different load types using parameters such as creep factor, shrinkage coefficient, curvature/strain factors, and deformation factors.

### Column structure
Each row contains:
- **Item**: parameter name
- **Description**: meaning and typical application
- **Unit**: unit column shown as “–” (dimensionless or unspecified in the extract)
- **Default**: default value provided in the table

### Parameter meanings and defaults (row by row)

- **NO** (Default: “–”):  
  The **number of the STAR2 computed load case** to be imported. Allowed range up to **max. 999**. No default is given because the load case must be selected explicitly.

- **PHI** (Creep factor, Default: **0**):  
  Governs the **creep factor** used when converting imported results into the corresponding creep-related strains/curvature-related load representation. In the text, special cases link **PHI** to creep deformation or constraints (e.g., **PHI = ϕ** for creep of a statically determinate load case; **PHI = -1.0** for constraints from a construction phase).

- **EPS** (Shrinkage coefficient, Default: **0**):  
  Controls the **shrinkage coefficient** contribution. In the associated formulation, **EPS** participates in forming strains/curvature loads.

- **FACV** (Factor for deformations, Default: **0**):  
  Scales an **affine initial deformation** derived from the stored elastic line. The table text explains that FACV can model effects such as undesired eccentricities; it also mentions different modeling opinions and that, since a given version, initial deformations are taken into account by displacements. If needed, previous initial deformations can be subtracted with **LCC and factor -1**.

- **FROM** (Range data for beam numbers, Default: **–**):  
  Start of the beam number range to import from. No default shown in the extract; it works together with **TO** to restrict which beams are loaded.

- **TO** (Default: **FROM**):  
  End of the beam number range. If TO is not specified, it defaults to **FROM**, meaning only one beam number/range point is targeted.

- **INC** (Default: **1**):  
  Increment/step for iterating through beam numbers when applying FROM/TO ranges. Default **1** implies consecutive beam numbers.

- **STIF** (Default: **NO**):  
  Load case number for **stiffnesses**. It likely determines which stiffness data are used during conversion/processing. Default equals **NO**, meaning stiffnesses correspond to the selected load case.

- **CSMI** (Lowest construction stage number, Default: **–**):  
  Lower bound for construction stage selection when importing/transforming results.

- **CSMA** (Highest construction stage number, Default: **CSMI**):  
  Upper bound for construction stage selection; defaults to **CSMI**, so the stage range can collapse to a single stage if CSMA isn’t given.

- **KTY P** (Loading type of prestress loads, Default: **SPL**):  
  Selects the variant of how prestress loads are represented. The table lists sub-options:
  - **SPL**: cubic variation  
  - **POL**: polygonal variation  
  - **SPL1**: cubic without secondary bending components  
  - **POL1**: polygonal without secondary bending components  
  The default is **SPL**.

Overall, this table is a configuration schema for LV: it specifies **which previous load case** to import (NO), **how strongly** and **in what manner** to translate its results into new loading (PHI/EPS/FACV), **which elements** to apply it to (FROM/TO/INC), **which stiffness reference** to use (STIF), optional **construction stage filtering** (CSMI/CSMA), and **prestress load representation style** (KTYPE).

The input table is a small parameter reference listing **two named factors (P9, P10, P11)** that influence calculations related to **strain and moment evaluation** and to **how outer reinforcement is interpreted** in the reinforced concrete design module (DESI/AQB/AQB-based operations as described in the accompanying text).

### Table structure
- **Columns:**  
  1) **Parameter** (e.g., “P9”)  
  2) **Description** (what the parameter controls)  
  3) **Default** (program default value)  
  4) **Typical** (typical recommended range used in practice)

### Rows / parameter meanings
1) **P9 – Factor for reference point of strain**
   - **Default:** `1.0`
   - **Typical:** `1.0`
   - **Interpretation:** Acts as a multiplier governing the **reference location used when calculating/iterating strain-related quantities**. Since both default and typical are 1.0, it is generally intended to remain unchanged unless a specialized calibration is required.

2) **P10 – Factor for reference point of moments**
   - **Default:** `1.0`
   - **Typical:** `0.2 – 1.0`
   - **Interpretation:** Controls the **reference point used for moment-related evaluation**, scaling how moments contribute at a chosen reference. The typical range indicates that, while 1.0 is the default, smaller values (down to ~0.2) may be used to adjust sensitivity or weighting in moment calculations.

3) **P11 – Factor for preference outer reinforcement**
   - **Default:** `*` (asterisk)
   - **Typical:** `0.0 – 1.0`
   - **Interpretation:** Determines the **preference/weighting given to outer reinforcement** in the model/calculation of reinforcement effects. The asterisk in the “Default” column means the default is not a single fixed numeric value; it likely depends on other conditions (e.g., bending mode), consistent with the surrounding text indicating different behavior for **biaxial vs uniaxial bending** (where P11 is described as varying: biaxial bending uses `1.0`, uniaxial bending uses `0.0`).

### Key takeaways for RAG use
- The table is a **parameter tuning guide** for strain and moment reference evaluation (**P9, P10**) and reinforcement preference (**P11**).
- **P9** is effectively fixed at 1.0.
- **P10** is usually between **0.2 and 1.0**.
- **P11** ranges **0.0–1.0**, with a non-numeric default (`*`) implying context-dependent default selection (e.g., dependent on bending conditions).

The input table defines configuration parameters for **reinforced concrete shear design** (record/keyword group that includes shear checks and truss/strut-and-tie model limits). Each row maps an **Item** (keyword), a **Description** explaining the engineering meaning and typical sub-options, a **Unit** describing expected input type, and a **Default** value indicating the system’s fallback behavior when the item is not explicitly provided.

Key parameters:

- **SMOD (Unit: LIT; Default: *) – Design mode shear.** Controls whether and how shear design is performed. Values include:
  - **NO**: no shear design.
  - Otherwise (implied by the mode system): activates the shear design workflow.

- **TVS (Unit: N/mm²; Default: *) – Deductional shear stress / stress limit.** Sets a shear stress limit used when applying deduction rules to shear capacity or checks.

- **MSCD (Unit: N/mm²; Default: *) – Maximum tensile longitudinal stress.** Limits the tensile longitudinal stress used for shear capacity reduction of tensile members.

- **KTAU (Unit: —/LIT; Default: *) – Shear design for plates.** Enables plate-related shear modeling; sub-options describe when design is “not staggered” or “staggered” for certain slab load/tributary conditions, following DIN 1045 17.5.5 conventions:
  - **K1**: not staggered for normal slabs (DIN 1045 17.5.5 equivalent, 14)
  - **K2**: not staggered for slabs with evenly distributed/tributary loading (… eq., 15)
  - **K1S**: like K1 but staggered
  - **K2S**: like K2 but staggered
  - **num**: coefficient *k* for EC2 equivalent, with example **4.18 EC2**
  - **0.0**: disables shear check

- **TTOL (Unit: —; Default: 0.02) – Tolerance for the limit values.** Specifies an allowable deviation when comparing computed stresses/limits.

- **TANA (Unit: —; Default: *) – Limits for inclination of struts of shear design.** Governs the allowable range of the truss strut angles (tangent form in related sections). The default is not explicitly fixed here (* indicates code-dependent or required input).

- **TANB (Unit: —; Default: *) – should be specified now with TVAR.** Indicates that TANA/TANB are legacy or coupled to another control record (**TVAR**) and should be handled via that mechanism.

- **SCL (Unit: —; Default: 3) – Plasticity control for steel and composite sections.** Integer flag selecting how plasticity/strain limitations are enforced:
  - **1**: no limits on steel strain
  - **2**: outermost compressive yield strain limited
  - **3**: compressive strain limited to yield value (default)
  - **4**: yield strain applied as limit in tensile and compressive regions

- **DELR (Unit: —; Default: 1.0) – Redistribution for ductiles x/D-Limit.** Global setting controlling redistribution behavior for ductility checks, with default factor 1.0.

Overall, the table is a parameterization layer: it selects the **shear design activation**, defines **stress limits and deduction rules**, configures **plate shear behavior** (including staggered/not-staggered approaches tied to DIN/EC2 concepts), and sets **tolerances and angle/strain/plasticity constraints** used in the shear/truss model.

Nodes and support conditions as well as all elements can be output. This is done by merely
 inputting the corresponding ECHO options NODE, BEAM, SPRI, BOUN or FULL. ECHO NODE FULL causes the additional output of the equation numbers of the degrees of freedom. This is helpful in detecting movable parts of the structure.
 Every time the equation system is reassembled, its parameters are output to the protocol file.

The beam internal forces and possibly the deformations are output for each section as well as for all positions, at which point loads are applied. The sign convention can be found in Section 2.2. In case of SECT and DEFO, YES results in a printout of values at explicit output sections only. Values at positions between sections where point loads are applied are printed using FULL. Values at all sections are printed using EXTR.
 Where applicable, the internal forces and deformations of springs, truss and cable elements are output.
 The displacements and rotations of nodes are output in mm and 0/00, respectively, in the directions of the coordinates. Rotations are positive clockwise.
 Forces arise at all nodes with supports, couplings or elastic foundations. These are output as follows:
 ECHO REAC YES only reactions ECHO REAC FULL reactions + coupling forces ECHO REAC EXTR
 all nodal forces (accuracy check)
 When forces are exerted on a free node, then either a support has been erroneously specified or the machine’s accuracy is not sufficient for solving the system.
 The sum of the reaction forces is an important index for the completeness of the loads.

A printout of the 1st iteration step (1st order theory) as well as a printout after the last step take place when nothing is input. If convergence is reached within the specified limits, its results are output too.
 Output after every nth step can be requested by ECHO STEP. The output of the initial linear analysis can be suppressed by using ECHO STEP -99.

It gets checked by every iteration step, whether the accuracy lies within the prescribed limits. This is performed separately for forces, moments, displacements and rotations. The procedure is the following:
 The difference between the result value during the current and the one during the pre- vious iteration is determined at each result point. This difference must be smaller than the absolute result value multiplied by the precision tolerance. If the value is smaller than the largest value encountered in the structure times the precision tolerance, the percentage difference is not computed. This way very small values, which e.g. oscil-
 late around zero from one iteration to the other, thus generating very high percentage changes, get no consideration at all.
 A summary of these values is printed at the beginning of each output iteration. These values are also output to the screen or to the protocol file for all iterations.

If the cross section is overstressed, RELTRA can be smaller than 1.0 as well. If the minimum reinforcement of the statically required cross sec- tion is critical, the internal forces are computed using the minimum reinforcement percentage, while the reinforcement is already reduced by the factor. The indication ”not recommended”
